text: A fintech company is building a customer-facing chat assistant that must respond to user messages in real time, with partial output appearing as it's generated to reduce perceived latency. The assistant also needs to handle occasional network interruptions gracefully without losing the user's place in a long response. Which combination of API features should the developer implement?
options: Use streaming responses via server-sent events, with client-side logic to handle reconnection and resume or restart partial generations on interruption
Use the Message Batches API with client polling every 500ms to simulate real-time incremental output
Use synchronous Messages API calls with max_tokens set very low to force frequent short responses
Use adaptive thinking mode exclusively, since it automatically buffers output and resends on network failure
correct_answer: Use streaming responses via server-sent events, with client-side logic to handle reconnection and resume or restart partial generations on interruption
explanation: Real-time, incremental display of model output is the core use case for Claude's streaming API (A), which delivers tokens via server-sent events as they're generated. Because network interruptions can occur mid-stream, production applications need client-side error handling to detect dropped connections and decide whether to resume, retry, or restart the request. The Message Batches API (B) is designed for asynchronous, non-interactive workloads (up to 24 hours) and is unsuitable for live chat. Lowering max_tokens (C) does not create real-time streaming behavior and would truncate responses. Adaptive thinking (D) is a reasoning mode, not a mechanism for connection resilience or streaming delivery.

text: A development team is modernizing a legacy monolithic application by gradually introducing Claude-powered features. They want to minimize regression risk, ensure each change can be independently reviewed and reverted, and keep the ability to roll back to a known-good state if a Claude integration causes unexpected behavior in production. Which practice best supports these goals?
options: Make all Claude integration changes directly on the main branch and deploy immediately after local testing
Rewrite the entire monolith in a single large commit so the Claude integration is complete and consistent from day one
Skip peer code review for AI-related changes since traditional review practices do not apply to non-deterministic LLM integrations
Use feature branches with incremental commits, pull request code review, and feature flags to gate the new Claude functionality, enabling isolated rollback if issues arise
correct_answer: Use feature branches with incremental commits, pull request code review, and feature flags to gate the new Claude functionality, enabling isolated rollback if issues arise
explanation: Core software engineering practices such as version control with feature branches, incremental small-scale changes, peer code review, and feature flags (D) reduce regression risk and allow teams to disable or revert a problematic Claude integration cleanly. Committing directly to main (A) and large-scale rewrites in a single commit (B) increase risk and make isolating failures difficult. LLM-related code changes still require the same engineering rigor as any other production code, so skipping review (C) is not appropriate.

text: A company deploys the same Claude-powered assistant across claude.ai (via a custom integration), the API directly in their backend, and Claude Desktop for internal employees. Users report inconsistent behavior: the assistant sometimes ignores instructions that work reliably in one interface but not another. Which design consideration is most likely responsible for this discrepancy?
options: Claude's underlying model weights differ depending on which client interface is used to send the request

Each interface may apply different system-level context, default instructions, or content boundaries, so instruction placement and interpretation can vary across Claude Code, Desktop, claude.ai, and direct API usage
Token limits are interface-specific and unrelated to prompt content, so this discrepancy is purely a billing issue
This is expected random variation from sampling settings and cannot be addressed through application or prompt design
correct_answer: Each interface may apply different system-level context, default instructions, or content boundaries, so instruction placement and interpretation can vary across Claude Code, Desktop, claude.ai, and direct API usage
explanation: A key Claude application design consideration is that Claude interprets instructions differently depending on the interface (B), since each surface (API, SDKs, Claude Code, Desktop, claude.ai) may layer in its own system prompts, default behaviors, tool harnesses, or content boundaries on top of user-supplied instructions. Developers must account for this when designing prompts intended to behave consistently across surfaces. The model weights themselves are not interface-specific (A), token limits are a separate axis unrelated to instruction-following behavior (C), and dismissing the issue as unaddressable randomness (D) ignores legitimate design-level causes and mitigations.

text: A platform team manages dozens of internal Claude applications built by different engineering groups. They want to ensure that when Anthropic releases a new model version, no application silently switches models and potentially breaks due to behavior changes, until each team has explicitly tested and approved the upgrade. Which configuration practice best achieves this?
options: Always reference an unpinned model alias so every application automatically receives the latest model as soon as it is released
Disable centralized configuration management and let each developer pass model identifiers ad hoc at request time

Pin each application to a specific, versioned model identifier in its configuration, and require teams to explicitly update that pinned version only after validating the new model against their test suite
Record model selection only in team runbooks rather than enforcing it in version-controlled code or configuration files
correct_answer: Pin each application to a specific, versioned model identifier in its configuration, and require teams to explicitly update that pinned version only after validating the new model against their test suite
explanation: Configuration management best practice for Claude applications includes model version pinning (C), which prevents unintended automatic upgrades when a new model is released. This gives teams control to validate behavior and API changes against their evaluation suite before adopting a new version. Using an unpinned alias (A) removes this control and risks silent breakage. Disabling configuration management (B) or relying on informal documentation (D) provides no enforceable, auditable control over which model version is running in production.

text: A business stakeholder requests a Claude-powered feature that 'summarizes customer support tickets automatically.' Before writing any code, the development team needs to translate this request into a concrete technical specification. Which set of considerations most directly reflects the 'Understanding Requirements' objective for Claude application development?
options: Clarifying input volume and format, expected latency and throughput needs, required output structure, integration points with existing ticketing systems, and relevant data handling or compliance constraints
Immediately selecting the lowest-cost model tier and the shortest possible system prompt to minimize initial development time
Finalizing the exact prompt wording first, then asking the stakeholder to approve it before considering any infrastructure or integration needs
Skipping upfront requirements gathering since Claude can adapt dynamically to any downstream system without specification
correct_answer: Clarifying input volume and format, expected latency and throughput needs, required output structure, integration points with existing ticketing systems, and relevant data handling or compliance constraints
explanation: Understanding requirements for a Claude application (A) involves translating business needs into functional and infrastructure requirements: input/output specifications, performance and scale expectations, integration points with existing systems, and compliance or data-handling constraints. This informs downstream decisions like model selection, API usage pattern (real-time vs. batch), and tool integration. Jumping straight to model selection (B) or prompt wording (C) without scoping requirements risks building the wrong solution, and skipping requirements analysis entirely (D) contradicts foundational systems life cycle practice.
